topic: California rejects Prop 40's one-time billionaire tax: a $100 billion health-care lifeline bought off, or a budget hole voters wisely refused?
question: Would Prop 40 really have raised about $100 billion, and did billionaire flight make it a net loser, as opponents said?
summary:
California voters turned down Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires living in the state on Jan. 1, 2026, with 90% of the money set aside for health care. With about three-quarters of ballots counted, No led roughly 53% to 47%; Los Angeles and San Francisco counties voted yes. The health-care union SEIU-UHW, backed by Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna, says it will return in 2028. The opposition was not only on the right: Sergey Brin put in $102 million, and Gov. Gavin Newsom, the teachers' union and Planned Parenthood's state affiliate also opposed it.

On the numbers, opponents had the firmer ground. The state's nonpartisan analysts projected 'tens of billions' and a likely ongoing income-tax loss of 'hundreds of millions of dollars or more per year.' The $100 billion figure depends on an assumption that only 10% would escape, and several of the richest billionaires had moved before the cutoff. Supporters are right that they were outspent about 10 to 1 and that federal Medicaid changes will cost many Californians coverage, but their '2 million' figure sits inside a wide range that includes the state's own cuts. Opponents' strongest warning, that founders' voting shares would be taxed far above their worth, rests on disputed wording.

The evidence cannot settle whether a one-time tax on wealth is fair, or how much flight the state should risk for it.
verdict: Roughly even, leaning slightly right on the checkable merits. 'Right' here means the measure's opponents, a coalition that included the Democratic governor. Their central fiscal claims match the Legislative Analyst's Office and the record of departures, though 'permanent hole' sets an ongoing loss against a large one-time gain without netting them. Supporters' spending and coverage-loss claims hold up, but their $100 billion headline leans on the most optimistic model. This says nothing about whether taxing wealth is just.
verificationNote: We read the Legislative Analyst's Office fiscal letter of Dec. 11, 2025 (primary), the initiative's voting-share text as quoted by the Tax Foundation, and UCLA's and CHCF's Medi-Cal projections directly. The economists' estimates come from NPR's Planet Money (read via member station WUNC; NPR's own page timed out) and City Journal; we could not read the underlying Hoover or Berkeley papers. Vote shares are preliminary and moved from 55.6% No at 60% counted to about 53% at 75%. The Hill, Forbes and Fox Business failed to load. We did not find a right-leaning outlet independently checking the Medi-Cal figures.
sources_consulted: UCLA Center for Health Policy Research
Supreme Court of the United States

left.label: Make billionaires pay for the health-care gap
left.framing: Washington is cutting Medicaid and millions of Californians stand to lose coverage. The state's few hundred billionaires hold trillions and pay little income tax relative to their wealth, so a one-time 5% levy could fill the gap. Voters were drowned out by billionaire money, and the fight returns in 2028.
left.strongestPoint: The spending gap was real and lopsided, and federal Medicaid changes really will remove large numbers of Californians from Medi-Cal. The Jan. 1 residency rule was a serious answer to the flight problem.
left.weakestPoint: The $100 billion headline relies on the most optimistic of the models and treats a one-time windfall as a fix for an ongoing coverage gap. Supporters waved off departures that had in fact happened among the very richest taxpayers.

right.label: A budget hole that drives out the tax base
right.framing: A one-time grab on paper wealth would push the state's biggest taxpayers out for good, swapping a temporary windfall for permanent income-tax losses. Its drafting would have punished founders who control their companies, and voters in a deep-blue state saw that.
right.strongestPoint: The state's own nonpartisan analysts confirmed the shape of the trade: a temporary gain of tens of billions and a likely ongoing income-tax loss, with departures by several of the richest billionaires already under way.
right.weakestPoint: 'Permanent hole' and the $39 billion net-loss figure count the ongoing loss heavily against the one-time gain under contested assumptions. The voting-share alarm was stated as fact when the drafters, and the text's own ambiguity, dispute it.

facts.claim: Prop 40 would raise about $100 billion for health care and other services.
facts.evidence: LAO: 'The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,' and 'The exact amount the state would collect is very hard to predict.' NPR: Saez, Zucman and Boll estimate 'about $100 billion,' after cutting projected revenue by 10% for avoidance and departures. Rauh and Jaros estimate 'around $30 billion.'
facts.explanation: $100 billion is the top of a wide range, produced by the proposal's own economists under a 10% avoidance assumption. The independent analysts did not endorse a number. Rauh, a Hoover economist and opponent, counts pre-cutoff departures that supporters say may not hold up legally. 'Up to $100 billion' would be fair; '$100 billion' as fact is not.

facts.claim: Prop 40 would create a lasting hole in the state budget through lost income-tax revenue.
facts.evidence: LAO: 'Likely ongoing decrease in state income tax revenues of hundreds of millions of dollars or more per year,' and 'that money would be temporary.' Building a Better California: 'it will create a permanent hole in the state budget.' Rauh: 'On net, the state loses $39 billion.' Zucman: 'You can't just count the loss and not the gain.'
facts.explanation: The ongoing loss is the state analysts' own finding, so the core claim holds. 'Hole' leaves out the one-time gain of tens of billions; whether the total is a net loss depends on contested modeling, which only Rauh's estimate answers yes. CalMatters reports the loss from departures at under $1 billion a year.

facts.claim: Billionaires had already left California before the tax could reach them.
facts.evidence: Fortune: Page, Brin, Thiel, Hankey, Kalanick and Spielberg moved before the Jan. 1 cutoff; together they 'would have collectively generated $27 billion.' City Journal: seven billionaires removed '$540 billion' in wealth, 'nearly 30%' of the base. Newsweek: Brin registered to vote in Nevada in December 2025.
facts.explanation: The moves are documented, but they are six or seven of roughly 200 billionaires, concentrated at the very top. Whether they ended California residency is disputed: Zucman says legal experts think it 'unlikely,' noting Brin still commutes. Spielberg's representative said his move was long planned. Zuckerberg left after the deadline.

facts.claim: Fears of tax flight are overblown; past taxes on the rich did not cause an exodus.
facts.evidence: Sociologist Cristobal Young, via AP: earlier California taxes on millionaires did not cause a mass exodus; 'they don't need to move somewhere else.' NPR: Norway's wealth-tax increases 'drove at most 100 rich people to leave.' Massachusetts's 2022 millionaires surtax brought in 'more than $3.1 billion in the first 10 months' of the fiscal year.
facts.explanation: The research on income-tax flight largely supports supporters. But Norway is a country, and NPR notes moving from California to Nevada is far easier. A wealth tax on a few hundred people is unlike a broad income tax, and departures by several of the very richest did happen here. Sound in general, weak for this case.

facts.claim: Federal cuts are set to push about 2 million Californians off health coverage, a gap Prop 40 would help fill.
facts.evidence: CalMatters: 'federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance.' DHCS, via CHCF: '1.1 million Medi-Cal enrollees will lose coverage by 2029–30 because of the H.R.1 work requirement.' UCLA: '2.98 million fewer Californians will be enrolled in Medi-Cal by 2028,' which it calls the high end.
facts.explanation: Large losses are real, and 2 million falls inside the range. But UCLA's total includes about 645,000 from the state's own budget choices, a freeze for undocumented adults and new premiums, not federal cuts. Lost Medi-Cal is not always lost insurance. The LAO adds that the tax money 'would be temporary,' while coverage costs recur.
facts.source: UCLA Center for Health Policy Research

facts.claim: The measure would tax founders on their voting control, far beyond the economic value of their shares.
facts.evidence: Initiative text, via the Tax Foundation: ownership 'shall be presumed to be not less than the taxpayer's percentage of the overall voting or other direct control rights.' Garry Tan: a 3% owner with 30% of votes would be presumed to own 30%. Drafters Galle, Gamage and Shanske: 'This is false, as shown by a straightforward reading.'
facts.explanation: The text plainly contains the presumption, and the Tax Foundation's Walczak calls the treatment 'so onerous it's unclear if this was intended.' Rep. Khanna, a supporter, reportedly conceded the language needed work. The drafters say fair market value governs. No court or agency ever ruled, so this is a live ambiguity, not an established effect.

facts.claim: Billionaire-funded opponents vastly outspent the measure's supporters.
facts.evidence: AP: opponents raised 'more than $300 million,' nearly a third from Brin; the SEIU-backed campaign raised $32.4 million. CalMatters: $316.7 million against, including Props 41 and 42. Newsweek: Brin 'has put $102 million into Building a Better California.'
facts.explanation: The gap was roughly 10 to 1. Spending does not by itself explain the result: the LA Times notes opposition ads featured teachers, nurses and firefighters, and the measure lost Democratic leaders such as Newsom. Support in the Berkeley IGS poll fell from 52% in March to 42% before the vote.

facts.claim: Voters in a deep-blue state decisively rejected the billionaire tax.
facts.evidence: Newsweek, about 60% counted: No 55.6%, Yes 44.4%. LA Times, about 75% counted: No about 53%, Yes 47%. Wikipedia tally at 75%: 5,456,978 No (53.37%) to 4,768,464 Yes (46.63%). LA Times: more than half of voters in Los Angeles and San Francisco counties backed it.
facts.explanation: The defeat is clear and the union conceded, but the margin narrowed as late ballots came in, so 'decisively' may overstate a roughly six-point loss. Results are not certified. The measure carried the two biggest urban counties.

powerLens.thesis: Both camps' views on where and how to tax great wealth track who holds the relevant power. Opponents call a one-time, backward-looking tax illegitimate, but a Republican Congress passed one in 2017. Democrats now say the fight 'belongs at the federal level,' yet when they held all of Washington in 2021 their billionaire tax died inside their own caucus.

precedent.case: The 2017 Mandatory Repatriation Tax, upheld in Moore v. United States (2024)
precedent.what: The Republican-passed Tax Cuts and Jobs Act imposed what the Supreme Court called 'a one-time, backward-looking, pass-through tax' on decades of foreign earnings never paid out to shareholders, at 8 to 15.5 percent. The Court upheld it 7-2 and left open whether income must be realized to be taxed. The free-market Competitive Enterprise Institute objected that it taxed 'income they never received.'
precedent.mirror: Prop 40 likewise looked back, to residency on Jan. 1, 2026, and taxed accumulated value. The mirror is imperfect: the 2017 tax reached profits a company had actually earned, not net worth. But 'retroactive' and 'one-time' were acceptable to its authors when the target was offshore corporate cash.
precedent.source: Supreme Court of the United States

flips.then: October 2021, with a Democratic House, Senate and White House: Sen. Wyden's billionaire tax on unrealized gains 'appeared scrapped' after Democratic Sen. Manchin objected, and House Ways and Means Chairman Neal said it 'may be difficult to implement.'
flips.now: June 2026, with Republicans holding Washington: Newsom, voting no on the state tax, wrote that 'The fight belongs at the federal level.' Pointing to the venue that is out of reach is a convenient place to park a principle.

flips.then: Republicans generally defend states' authority over their own tax policy and, in 2017, enacted a one-time backward-looking federal tax on accumulated earnings.
flips.now: 2026: Rep. Kevin Kiley (R-Calif.) introduced a bill to bar any state from imposing a retroactive tax on former residents: 'No state should be allowed to reach back in time and impose a new tax on someone who no longer lives there.' Federal override of a state's voters is an odd fit with federalism.

corroboration.source: Supreme Court of the United States

powerLens.longRun: Strip out the labels and the durable through-line is that taxing the very rich is popular in the abstract and fragile in the specific. Whoever controls the venue that could act tends to find reasons not to, and whoever does not points to it. Expect Democrats to discover new federal problems with a billionaire tax if they regain the White House, and Republicans to rediscover states' rights once a red state wants a tax the left dislikes.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Both sides lose some reasoning credit: supporters' Democratic allies for invoking a federal fix they did not pass when they could, opponents for treating retroactivity as beyond the pale while defending the 2017 precedent. The needle rests on the revenue, departure, spending and coverage facts above, not on these flips.

pattern.thesis: Prop 40 is the latest in a run of ballot measures taxing top earners, and treating it as a one-off referendum on 'billionaires' hides the trend. Voters have backed some such taxes and rejected others, and the outcome often turns less on whether the rich should pay than on who designs the tax, who funds the campaign and where the money goes.

campaigns.what: A 1.75% tax on incomes above $2 million for electric-vehicle subsidies and wildfire work, funded mostly by Lyft. Newsom called it 'a taxpayer-funded giveaway to rideshare companies.' Voters rejected it, about 59% to 41%.

Voters approved a 4% surtax on income above about $1 million, dedicated to education and transportation. Lawmakers budgeted about $1 billion; it brought in about $3 billion in fiscal 2025 and more than $3.1 billion in ten months of fiscal 2026.
A first-ever one-time state tax on billionaires' net worth, opposed by $300 million-plus and by the Democratic governor; trailing about 53% to 47% at 75% counted.

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question: is a tax on the rich being judged on its design and destination, or on the label? Income surtaxes with broad purposes have passed; novel or narrowly targeted ones have failed, sometimes with Democratic leaders leading the opposition. The 'one-off' tell is reading Prop 40's defeat as a verdict on taxing the rich in general, or its 47% as proof voters want a wealth tax.

notAdjudicable: Whether taxing accumulated wealth, rather than income, is fair is a moral question about desert and property that no revenue estimate can answer.
How much risk of losing wealthy residents a state should accept to fund health care is a trade-off of values, not a checkable fact.
Whether concentrated fortunes threaten democracy, or represent earned rewards for building companies, depends on contested views of merit and power.
Whether health care for low-income residents should be paid for by a narrow group or by broad taxes is a judgment about who owes what.
Whether heavy spending by billionaires in a ballot campaign is legitimate speech or undue influence is a values dispute about money in politics.
biasWatch: The bias here is the anchoring effect: each side fixed on one number and argued from it. Supporters anchored on $100 billion, the most optimistic estimate; opponents on a $39 billion net loss, the most pessimistic. The state's neutral analysts declined to give either figure, saying only 'tens of billions' and an ongoing loss of 'hundreds of millions or more.' The tell: when someone states a single precise figure for a tax that has never been tried, ask who produced the model and what share of the rich it assumed would leave. Watch too for the reverse halo: some opponents treat the measure as wrong because billionaires backed defeating it, others because a union wrote it. Neither fact settles what it would have raised.
